title: Joshua 17:14–18
context: The tribes of Joseph complain that one lot is too small for so numerous a people. Joshua, himself from Ephraim (Numbers 13:8), answers by turning their complaint back on them: if they are many and strong, they should clear the forested hill country and trust God to give victory over the Canaanites with iron chariots.

verses.text: The children of Joseph spoke to Joshua, saying, “Why have you given me just one lot and one part for an inheritance, since we are a numerous people, because the LORD has blessed us so far?”
verses.arminianNotes: The tribes of Joseph acknowledge that the LORD has blessed them, yet they complain that one lot is not enough. Arminian readers see a familiar human tendency to measure blessing by size and to ask for more rather than steward what has been given.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Joseph’s children speak of God’s blessing but turn it into an argument for privilege. The verse exposes how even gratitude can be mixed with a sense of entitlement, which Joshua will gently confront.

verses.text: Joshua said to them, “If you are a numerous people, go up to the forest, and clear land for yourself there in the land of the Perizzites and of the Rephaim, since the hill country of Ephraim is too narrow for you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua takes them at their word: if they are numerous, they can clear the forest and expand. Arminian readers see a leader who calls people to use their God-given strength rather than wait for an easier gift.
verses.reformedNotes: Joshua does not grant special favor even to his own tribe. Reformed readers see godly leadership refusing partiality, and pointing the people back to what God has already given them, with the work it requires.

verses.text: The children of Joseph said, “The hill country is not enough for us. All the Canaanites who dwell in the land of the valley have chariots of iron, both those who are in Beth Shean and its towns, and those who are in the valley of Jezreel.”
verses.arminianNotes: The tribes object that the hill country is too small and the valley Canaanites have iron chariots. Arminian readers note that fear of the enemy’s strength echoes the unbelief of the spies at Kadesh (Numbers 13:31-33).
verses.reformedNotes: Iron chariots were a real military advantage, and Judges 1:19 records that Judah could not drive out valley dwellers who had them. Reformed readers see the objection as measuring God’s promise by human resources, a recurring failure in Israel’s story.

verses.text: Joshua spoke to the house of Joseph, that is, to Ephraim and to Manasseh, saying, “You are a numerous people, and have great power. You shall not have one lot only;
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua affirms that the house of Joseph is numerous and powerful and will not have one lot only. Arminian readers see encouragement that respects their capacity and calls them to act on it with faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Joshua’s reply grants their claim about their size but redirects it toward responsibility. Reformed readers see in this a pastoral wisdom that affirms God’s blessing while refusing to let it become an excuse for inaction.

verses.text: but the hill country shall be yours. Although it is a forest, you shall cut it down, and it’s farthest extent shall be yours; for you shall drive out the Canaanites, though they have chariots of iron, and though they are strong.”
verses.arminianNotes: The forest can be cleared, and the Canaanites can be driven out despite their chariots. Arminian readers stress that the promise is real but requires effort and trust, a pattern they see throughout Scripture for those who would lay hold of God’s gifts.
verses.reformedNotes: Joshua grounds his confidence in God’s promise rather than in Israel’s strength: you shall drive out the Canaanites, though they are strong. Reformed readers see here the assurance that God’s word is sure, even when his people must labor to see it fulfilled.
